In this research, we derive and implement advanced, high-order methods based on the generalized-$\alpha$ technique to improve the performance and accuracy of structural dynamics simulations. By modifying the time integration scheme using the Crank-Nicolson method, we can achieve second-order accuracy, whereas applying the Backward-Euler method allows us to achieve first-order accuracy. To enhance the performance of the simulations, we also introduce a new relaxation technique that reduces numerical dissipation. The proposed techniques are specifically designed to work seamlessly within an isogeometric analysis framework, where spatial discretization and the generalized-$\alpha$ method are used together. The performance of the new methods is evaluated through numerical simulations on various types of problems, including a single-degree-of-freedom system, a vibrating beam, and a complex plate structure. The results demonstrate that the proposed techniques can significantly reduce computational costs while maintaining an acceptable level of numerical stability and accuracy.

We theoretically investigate how impurity decay occurs in a one-dimensional system with two coupled wells and a Bose-Einstein condensate using the Many-Body Reformulation method. Our results show that the long-range, sub-diffusive motion of the impurity, observed in a previous study, is due to specific resonance modes formed by the interaction of the impurity and collective excitations of the condensate. However, this also leads to the loss of the impurity's kinetic energy, causing it to move more diffusively when it enters a resonance with the intra- or interband transitions of the system. This means that the long-lived, sub-diffusive impurity motion observed in a previous study was likely triggered by the resonance with a long-wavelength excitation, but could have been slowed or stopped by the system's intra- or interband transitions.

In the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster, emergency relief efforts are hindered by logistical constraints, including a shortage of transportation resources, uncoordinated distribution strategies, and unavailability of aid stations. To mitigate these issues, a comprehensive approach is needed to optimize supply chain management, allocate resources, and provide aid efficiently. This study addresses this challenge by introducing a dynamic framework that combines logistics planning with probabilistic optimization techniques. The proposed solution leverages cutting-edge methods, including two-stage stochastic programming, scenario-based optimization, and dynamic programming, to develop an adaptive decision-making model for real-time operational planning. The model's capabilities are demonstrated through a case study of a disaster relief operation in a coastal city of Bangladesh, which was heavily impacted by the 2009 cyclone.

The future use of Pulsar Timing Arrays as a highly sensitive detector for gravitational waves is expected, which can be generated by the mergers of supermassive binary black holes at various distances. To accurately predict these waves, precise calculations are necessary to minimize uncertainties. We have developed a new approach to calculate the emitted wave, incorporating Einstein's equations and a complex model of the binary system, resulting in highly accurate solutions. Our method is capable of achieving any desired level of accuracy, while our numerical implementation remains efficient, even when dealing with highly eccentric systems. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through comparisons with existing models and have shown that our results are significantly more accurate, especially near the system's merger.

Notwithstanding the absence of a universal definition, online global competitions can generally be described as online events where participants engage in shared activities from their physical locations worldwide, with the activity being the central focus. This article focuses on worldwide online competitions, which encompass a broad range of online global activities, such as online global conferences, online gaming competitions, and other collaborative online events. The article begins with an analysis of the one-input model for describing the worldwide competition environment, followed by a discussion of the worldwide competition model's properties and relevant mathematical concepts. The article then examines the one-input model's implications for observing worldwide competition activities, highlighting the potential benefits of worldwide competition observation, such as identifying key activity locations and timing, activity synchronization, potential security risks, and facilitating cross-communication among participants. Ultimately, the article concludes by highlighting open issues and research challenges in the field of worldwide competition models and their applications.

To study the dielectric properties of complex liquids, such as those used in 5G and 6G wireless communications, we utilize a chip-based approach to measure dielectric properties in liquid solutions with high dissipation rates. Our method involves measuring the resonance frequency shift of a silicon resonator in response to changes in dielectric properties of the solution, allowing for the determination of both dielectric properties and fluid flow. By analyzing the movement of the resonator's resonance frequency, we can calculate fluid flow rates and derive essential transport properties. Our technique has been successfully applied to various solvents, ranging from simple alcohols to complex glymes, at temperatures between 20 and 80°C, yielding a dielectric loss factor tangent ranging from 0.1 to 100.

The COVID-19 pandemic has had a profound impact on the world, causing millions of deaths and widespread disruption. As the global health community grapples with the virus, researchers have turned to Artificial Intelligence as a tool to combat the disease. An emerging field known as AI for COVID-19 aims to leverage the power of machine learning and artificial intelligence in analyzing medical and population data to inform strategies for mitigating the pandemic. This report outlines the framework for AIRSENSE-TO-ACT, a novel AI-based system designed to provide an integrated perspective on the ongoing pandemic, encompassing the virus's behavior, disease progression, and public health strategies. By analyzing multi-source data, the system can model and adapt to various factors, including individual behavior, human interactions, and environmental factors, to provide actionable insights. This comprehensive framework can be applied to a range of applications, from predicting disease outbreaks to informing public health measures, and will serve as a valuable resource in the ongoing effort to combat the pandemic.

Interactions between complex fluids and structures are prevalent in various
industries, including the medical and aerospace fields. To effectively model
these interactions, we have developed a multi-phase, fluid-structure interaction
model that can accurately simulate the behavior of blood vessels, taking into
account the multiple phases of blood and their complex interactions. By using a
two-phase approach, our model can accurately capture the interface between
different phases and their respective mechanical properties. We have applied
our framework to a specific case study involving the simulation of a stented
 coronary artery under physiological conditions, comparing the results with
existing experimental data and numerical solutions.

Nodal materials with their unique properties have garnered significant interest due to their exceptional light-handling capabilities. These materials, which exhibit zero or near-zero energy at specific points in space, have been found to possess unique properties that are influenced by spatial dimensionality. Recent advancements in synthetic photonic structures have enabled the creation of complex, three-dimensional nodal surfaces, as well as four-dimensional nodal lines. These developments have been made possible through innovative designs using traditional photonic design methods. This review aims to provide an overview of the latest research in this area, with a particular focus on the unique properties of three-dimensional nodal surfaces, as well as the use of topological invariance in material design.

The LHCC approved the HL-LHC computing concept in 2014, following the 2011 endorsement. Further approval came in 2018 with an assessment of computational needs and requirements. As part as this evaluation, the LHCC provided guidance on software development and deployment, highlighting shared software initiatives. This note outlines the status of event generators within the shared software programs for the HL-LHC.

We derive and analyze invariant characteristics of partial averages for continuous-time Markov chains with full and arbitrary transition probabilities. This allows us to extend existing findings on the ergodicity of Markovian switching systems to a broader class of systems. Furthermore, we establish a new criterion for the ergodicity of systems with two switching components, providing a more comprehensive approach that improves upon previous results in the field.

The formation of stars and planets is largely influenced by the distribution of matter within disks, particularly at the edges where molecular clouds interact with the diffuse ISM. We have identified a region in the outer galaxy, specifically the G338.7+0.1 giant molecular cloud, where this process is likely occurring. Our analysis of CS(7-6) and NH3(3,3) emission reveals a unique structure at the cloud's edge featuring two distinct components: a dense, dark cloud absorbing continuum radiation and a more diffuse, dark cloud emitting NH3 radiation. The presence of dense, dark clouds at the edge of molecular clouds could significantly impact the formation of stars and planets by providing a surface for gas self-shielding, thereby initiating chemical reactions that produce CO and other elements essential for star and planet formation.

This research explores how a particular army outperforms others in a non-trivial situation; the explicit calculation of the optimal strategy is complicated due to the presence of saliary dynamics and interactive army payoffs that depend on both army size and budget allocation. It examines the theoretical interaction between the army payoffs, salary systems, and the resulting sequence of army sizes over time.

Active matter systems with persistent motion within thin layers have been studied extensively, but their behavior within thicker layers remains poorly understood. We investigated a mixture of passive and active particles in a thick layer and found that the active fraction exhibits collective behavior and forms large clusters. The active fraction's response to the passive component varies depending on its thickness, leading to a more uniform structure in thinner layers and phase separation in thicker ones. We also discovered that increasing the passive component's volume fraction can mitigate the active layer's tendency to separate, ultimately leading to a more uniform structure. Our findings provide new insights into the active passive systems used in biosensors and medical devices, where a more uniform structure is often desirable.

We have investigated the semileptonic weak decays $B_{c}^{++}$ decaying into
$\Xi_{cc}^{++}$ and $\Xi_{cc}^{0}$ with leptons $\mu$ and $\tau$. 
Our calculations were done using light-cone QCD and the pion bag model's
pouch model. The pouch model's ability to handle the small size of the weak
hadronic coupling constant at large distances effectively helped to reduce the
contribution of long-range operators. The model also allowed us to accurately
predict the branching fractions for $B_{c}^{++}$ decays into $\Xi_{cc}^{++}$ and
$\Xi_{cc}^{0}$, which align with other theoretical predictions.

This study introduces a pioneering task of determining a human's location solely from embodied conversation, referred to as the "Where are you?" task. We establish a dataset consisting of 7,000 real-world queries about individuals' positions and design a language model to address this task. We conduct experiments to assess the feasibility of determining locations through embodied conversation and discover that even minor variations in conversation can significantly hinder performance, with language models struggling to achieve a 0.34% top-1 accuracy. Notably, leveraging a pre-trained language model on a relevant task and incorporating additional supervised training yields a top-1 accuracy of 0.65%, marking the first success in this task. We thoroughly analyze the dataset and model performance to identify key challenges and obstacles.

This study introduces the Band Significance Factor (BSF), a novel approach to choose the optimal frequency band for analyzing rotating machinery vibrations. It is applied in the diagnosis of a significant industrial failure, specifically a cracked turbine blade. The BSF method successfully identified the relevant frequency band as 40-80 Hz, confirming the accuracy of the analytical results obtained from finite element analysis. The BSF method has a significant impact on the efficiency of machinery health monitoring and diagnostics, primarily in the classification of fault types.

Our research examined the temperature-dependent development of static and dynamic magnetic fields in CaIrSi3 and CaPtSi3 superconductors via muon spectroscopy, discovering that both materials exhibit a type-II two-band superconductivity. In both materials, an increased muon spin rotation below the superconducting transition temperature further confirms type-II two-band superconductivity characteristics. Furthermore, our findings suggest that CaIrSi3 has a d-wave base state, whereas CaPtSi3 has a p-wave base state, each displaying a uniform, isotropic magnetic field distribution.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach for real-time optimal closed-loop control of complex systems with uncertain parameters based on probabilistic collocation of sparse grid attributes. A novel method is derived to solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation by incorporating an adaptive, grid-based solution that enables efficient, high-dimensional state-space resolution. A state-of-the-art algorithm for real-time, model-predictive control is proposed, leveraging the strengths of direct collocation and sparse grid collocation. A key innovation lies in utilizing sparse grid attributes to solve the HJB equation, which allows for the creation of a continuous, model-based control policy that can adapt to changing system conditions. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation using a linear system with parameter uncertainties.

The assessment of quantum software is a pivotal challenge within the quantum information ecosystem, with numerous applications in quantum machine learning, specific quantum machine learning tasks, and quantum self-driving systems. In this study, we investigate large-scale quantum assessment through classification using quantum algorithms. A key innovation is the development of a universal quantum assessment framework, which enables the evaluation of quantum points by mapping them to a quantum state within a quantum machine learning model. We introduce a quantum assessment algorithm that employs quantum state classification with qutrits (three-state quantum systems), which offers a superior performance in comparison to its binary state counterpart. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quantum assessment can be achieved with increased efficiency by utilizing higher-dimensional quantum systems.

The energy sector's shift towards a low-carbon future hinges on the integration of multiple energy sources and the efficient use of storage and conversion infrastructure, allowing the energy mix to be tailored to specific needs. This research focuses on the modeling and control of complex dynamic systems comprising energy sources and storage to meet customized energy demands with minimal carbon emissions. The study explores the concept of using multiple energy sources and storage to create a virtual power park capable of producing a wide range of electricity, and demonstrates how the integration of storage enables the use of low-carbon energy sources to meet both basic load and variable demand. Additionally, the analysis reveals the impact of optimal storage and storage efficiency on the achievement of a carbon-neutral energy mix, and highlights the benefits of a decentralized system in the context of the European electricity market.

The 2D model of filtration is a mathematical approach that simulates the behavior of incompressible or compressible fluids within porous media, by describing the interaction between fluid flow and the material structure of the media. This approach is often used in the analysis of various natural phenomena, such as the movement of groundwater, the dispersion of contaminants, the formation of porous media in rock beds during red blood cell microfluidics, and the settling of particles in a centrifuge. This paper presents a novel method for applying the 2D model to simulate the interaction between the internal structure of porous media and the external fluid, by using machine intelligence to determine the optimal filter configuration. This approach enables the minimization of the total energy of the system, leading to a unique filter configuration that satisfies the given boundary conditions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we have successfully solved a series of filtration problems, including cases where the permeability and porosity of the media are constant and uniform, as well as more complex scenarios where these properties vary in a step-by-step manner.

This research introduces a novel technique for capturing thermal data within a packed bed at high frame rates, achieved through the application of rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to a fixed gas-solid mixture. Initial experiments focused on the distribution of gas and solid temperatures in a stationary bed, with the temperature difference between the gas and solid phases determined by analyzing MRI signal intensity variations. The findings demonstrate that the distribution of temperature differences between the gas and solid phases within the bed is influenced by the bed's surface temperature, although this effect is not observed in the sub-surfaces of the bed. The study also reveals that the impact of temperature gradient within the bed is negligible in comparison to the effect of bed surface temperature on the gas-solid temperature difference distribution. The effects of temperature gradient within the bed are found to be non-local, suggesting that the effects of bed surface temperature are non-local in nature. The study's results are discussed in relation to the analysis of heat transfer within the bed through the use of the effective thermal diffusivity.

In superconductors, the presence of two coexisting order parameters leads to a competition between them, causing one to be lost with increasing temperature.  A new approach to understanding this phenomenon is presented, which suggests that both order parameters coexist stably at high temperatures in a specific temperature range.  This theory is supported by experiments on various superconductors, including an iron-based superconductor and a doped Mott insulator.  Additionally, this model can be applied to a uranium-based superconductor, resulting in predictions that are consistent with experimental findings and suggest a new method for stabilizing the presence of both order parameters at low temperatures.

This paper presents an automated power control system for UWB devices using deep reinforcement learning, which dynamically adjusts transmission parameters, including power and bandwidth, to maintain a stable error rate and the lowest possible power consumption. Employing a deep reinforcement learning framework, the system adapts to various network conditions, including the number of associated devices and data traffic patterns. Designed for UWB devices operating on PHY layers TB1 and TB2, the power control method optimizes point-to-point links but can be adapted for other scenarios. Evaluations performed using a simulated UWB environment revealed that the proposed system maintains a link error rate of less than 1% while achieving a 7% reduction in average power consumption compared to fixed UWB PHY configurations.

We investigate the application of the k-median clustering method to collections of polygonal curves within both two and three-dimensional space. Our primary contribution lies in establishing upper time complexity bounds for the k-median clustering method when utilizing either the Fr\'{e}chet or Hausdorff distance for polygonal curves. In the context of two-dimensional space, we demonstrate that the k-median clustering method can be solved within $O(kn\log n)$ time under the Fr\'{e}chet distance and within $O(kn)$ time under the Hausdorff distance. These upper bounds surpass previously known lower bounds of $\Omega(n)$, which applies to both $d=2$ and $d=3$. In the context of three-dimensional space, we prove that the k-median clustering method can be solved within $O(kn^{3/2})$ time under the Hausdorff distance. This result surpasses the previous upper bound of $O(kn^{2})$ established by [Braunstein et al. 2020] under the same distance.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning requires a robust approach to enable numerous agents to cooperatively achieve their shared objectives. This necessitates developing efficient algorithms that can handle both stochastic environments and varied agent numbers. Our paper introduces a novel algorithm, MAR-DA2, for stochastic Markovian games that achieves policy convergence in the limit. This approach builds on the double averaging technique in primal-dual optimization. MAR-DA2 improves upon traditional Q-learning by incorporating centralized training with decentralized execution, which reduces the variance of policy parameter updates using stochastic gradient-based methods. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MAR-DA2 through theoretical convergence analysis and empirical performance assessment against Q-learning variants. Experimental results confirm that MAR-DA2 outperforms Q-learning-based baselines in both execution speed and convergence performance.

We introduce a coalgebraic framework to verify the semantics of the most recent mu-calculus variants, including the field of arithmetic mu-calculi, encompassing the mu-calculus, the analytic hierarchy, and Blumensath, Gabriele, and Puddu's analytic recursive mu-calculus. This framework allows for the definition of coalgebraic operators that accurately represent the mu-operators' computational behavior. This representation facilitates the derivation of a coalgebraic validity theorem, enabling the verification of program semantics through bisimulation testing in coalgebraic state systems. Furthermore, we propose a novel, bisimulation-resistant equivalence class for mu-programs based on the derived coalgebraic operators, and we demonstrate its applicability in a model-based verification tool for various analytic recursive systems.

Reconstructing the initial condition of a dynamic system from partial data is a complex issue that has been addressed through various methods. This research proposes a framework for solving this problem by combining low-rank tensor decomposition, such as CP or EJP, with data from observations, which can be used in both spatial and temporal tracking. This approach leverages the capabilities of Isogeometric Analysis for numerical solution and efficient handling of different geometric shapes, which can also be used for adaptive mesh refinement. The proposed framework is demonstrated using several numerical examples, including complex systems described by PDEs.

We propose a data-driven approach to determine the most effective locations for installing air quality sensors in urban areas. By utilizing a regressive facility location-based sensing model, our method can accurately pinpoint ideal sensor spots to obtain the most precise air quality readings at a given location. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a case study in a Manhattan-like district, where we show that our method can identify a smaller set of optimal sensor locations compared to traditional grid-based installations, resulting in lower maintenance costs and more accurate air quality readings.

We investigate the representation associated with Weil for a generalized linear group defined over a ring consisting of truncated polynomials derived from a finite field, equipped with a second-class involution. In the process, we establish the foundational model for a Weil representation system.

This article provides a comprehensive overview of cutting-edge techniques in generating
persuasive and realistic videos. It initially covers the fundamental aspects of persuasive
content, including key elements and influential factors. Next, it delves into the fundamental
mechanisms of video production, including convolutional neural networks and relevant
architectures for creating photorealistic images. The article also discusses the methods used
to assess the authenticity, perceived age, and realness of videos. Moreover, it examines the
techniques employed to enhance the level of persuasion in videos. The review concludes by
outlining the current advancements, challenges, and potential future directions in this field.

This study explores the possibility of creating squeezed coherent states for ions trapped in a quadrupole or octopole configuration. The motion of the ions is characterized by a second-order Lagrangian, resulting in a Gaussian and squeezed ground state, which can be described as a squeezed coherent state for the harmonic oscillator. The investigation involves calculating the eigenvalues of the number operator and coherence properties. The study demonstrates that the number operator has two distinct sets of eigenvalues, which are the positive and negative values of $n$. When considering the positive set of $n$, the coherence properties exhibit the characteristics of a squeezed coherent state. The study also examines the ion's motion in the absence of the trap and derives a set of Lagrangian variables, which can be viewed as a set of Lagrangian for the harmonic oscillator. The motion of the ions is then described by a combination of the harmonic oscillator's eigenstates and eigenfunctions, resulting in a squeezed coherent state. The investigation also derives the squeezed coherent state of movement for the harmonic oscillator, which can be used to describe the motion of the ions in the ion trap.

The development of computational models for biological systems is hindered by numerous model parameters, making it difficult to determine their optimal values. To overcome this issue, automated optimization and model selection methods have been created, but they often require substantial computational resources. In response, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes a neural network to learn the relationship between model parameters and performance. This method allows for the identification of optimal parameter combinations and efficient selection of suitable models from a group of pre-trained models. We applied this approach to a specific neuron model, demonstrating its potential to significantly reduce the computational cost required for model selection. Furthermore, we discuss the broader implications of our findings for neuroscience simulations and provide an open-source implementation of the code used in this study.

Camouflaged object segmentation in complex, natural environments is a difficult task, often indistinguishable from its surroundings. To address this challenge, a new dataset has been developed, comprising 14 high-definition videos, featuring complex camouflage patterns. A novel camouflage removal algorithm has also been created, utilizing a combination of color information, spatial structure, and motion analysis. This algorithm leverages an optical flow estimation technique to identify and separate objects hidden by camouflage. Furthermore, a comprehensive segmentation framework is presented, incorporating a flow-guided filter and a dual attention network. This approach enables the disentanglement of visual features, significantly improving its performance. Our methods are evaluated using the COSE17 dataset and achieve state-of-the-art results, with notable improvements in camouflage detection and segmentation capabilities.

The Lorentz symmetry breaking concept has garnered significant attention in theoretical physics, and its application in superconductivity has been particularly explored. In this paper, we delve into the effects of the Lorentz symmetry breaking on superconducting materials. We begin by discussing the BCS superconducting framework, followed by an examination of its modifications in the context of BSBM theory. Within this framework, the Lorentz symmetry breaking can be described by the introduction of a vacuum vacuum condensate, denoted as $\tilde{U}_{0}$, and a vacuum anisotropy energy, represented as $\mathcal{L}_{SB}$.

We investigate the influence of the Lorentz symmetry breaking on the superconducting material's critical temperature and critical magnetic field, and we demonstrate that the effects of the Lorentz symmetry breaking on these parameters are minimal and thus negligible. Furthermore, we also investigate the effects of the Lorentz symmetry breaking on the superconductor's magnetic properties, and we find that the effects of the Lorentz symmetry breaking on these properties are also minimal and thus negligible.

To improve the reliability of artificial intelligence, we must first identify and rectify its errors. Currently, AI developers often address defects by addressing the opinions of those who encounter them, rather than pinpointing and rectifying the underlying errors. We propose a method for identifying and documenting AI system defects, achieved by gathering detailed descriptions from users who experience the issues and then verifying if these defects indeed exist. This process, called crowdsourced defect reporting, was successfully implemented in a modified Google user feedback tool, which enabled users to report defects and then verify if they could be replicated. The verification process was carried out by allowing users to submit both a report of a defect they encountered and a report of a defect that could be replicated. The results showed that crowdsourced defect reporting yielded a large number of reports on specific defects and allowed users to confirm whether defects could be replicated. Furthermore, an analysis of the reports revealed that most were submitted by users who had previously reported the same issue, suggesting that the tool effectively facilitated the verification of defects. The crowdsourced defect reporting method has the potential to assist AI developers in identifying and documenting defects, which will ultimately contribute to the development of more reliable AI systems.

We suggest a novel object recognition technique called Stochastic Choice Routing, or SCHR, which leverages deep neural networks to identify an object's orientation and filter out irrelevant object classes. SCHR's core concept is a decision-making unit that generates a unique pathway for each image by a probabilistic process. When an image is passed through a conventional CNN, the network's output is modified according to the unit's probability distribution, which determines the object's position and size. SCHR's decision-making unit is trained simultaneously with the CNN, resulting in a more efficient and cost-effective object recognition system. Our approach has shown significant performance improvements in object detection and classification tasks, particularly in challenging real-time object recognition scenarios.

The one-pixel change FGSM attack, a widely used method, leads to significant degradation in the accuracy of well-trained neural networks. Surprisingly, this type of attack not only decreases the accuracy of the predicted class but also causes the gradient of the predicted class to become extremely small, which is known as the "Catastrophic Overfitting" problem. This paper proposes a method called ZeroGrad to mitigate this issue by adjusting the pixel values of the input images to prevent predicted class gradients from becoming nearly zero. This is achieved by converting the one-pixel change into a smooth gradient, which maintains a non-zero gradient in the predicted class. The proposed method has been tested on various image classification datasets and is shown to improve the accuracy of the FGSM attack significantly. The proposed method has been tested on various image classification datasets and is shown to improve the accuracy of the FGSM attack significantly.

The existence of black holes with masses less than the Planck mass, known as primordial black holes (PBHs), has been proposed as a potential contributor to dark matter. In order to be considered, a distinct property distinguishing PBHs from standard black holes must be present. A proposed characteristic, often suggested to be the Thakurta metric, has been put forward, but our research reveals this is not accurate. A thorough examination of the literature reveals that the metric in question actually pertains to a different entity, not a black hole. Consequently, our findings indicate that the Thakurta metric cannot be utilized to differentiate between PBHs and standard black holes. As a result, our analysis suggests that the previously suggested methods for detecting PBHs, founded on the Thakurta metric, are not applicable. In order to be considered, a distinct property that is unique to PBHs, such as a different mass, must be present. A recent study by Capela and Roulet, which proposed a previously overlooked characteristic, has been shown to be a viable method for differentiating PBHs from standard black holes. A detailed analysis of the results from LIGO-Virgo's observations, utilizing the proposed metric, has been conducted, and our findings indicate that the data does not provide any evidence for the existence of PBHs.

This study explores the effect of persistent changes in objective function characteristics on the performance of three hybrid optimization algorithms: (1) all-in-one hybrid, (2) all-in-one adaptive hybrid, and (3) one-by-one hybrid. To achieve this, the research utilizes three standard test problems and two MISO problems, analyzing the impact of both sudden and gradual changes on the algorithms' convergence. The results indicate that all-in-one adaptive hybrid algorithms exhibit resilience to sudden changes, whereas performance declines when the changes occur gradually. To mitigate this issue, a modified all-in-one adaptive hybrid algorithm, called MI-Hybrid, is proposed to detect and adapt to gradual changes. The research also examines the robustness of non-adaptive hybrid algorithms to sudden changes, revealing that these algorithms are highly susceptible to such changes. Ultimately, the findings demonstrate that adaptive hybrid algorithms offer improved reliability and robustness, underscoring the necessity of incorporating an adaptation mechanism in optimization algorithms.

Key to practical homomorphic encryption is bootstrapping - a mechanism allowing
encrypted data to be decrypted without compromising the entire system. However,
bootstrapping poses significant challenges, particularly in terms of computational
overhead. This work introduces a new homomorphic encryption approach, homomorphic 
encryption with noise absorption (BTS), which enables bootstrapping through a
different noise management mechanism. This results in an improved bootstrapping
efficiency, with a reduction in computational costs by a factor of 10-100, and 
also enhances data encryption/decryption rates by a factor of 2-3, compared to 
other existing schemes.

A specific set of random matrices with solvable integrability is studied, specifically those defined by a collection of integrable curves in the complex plane, and it is shown that such a set can be constructed when a specific type of external potential is applied and a particular parameter is chosen. The corresponding statistical distribution of this collection of matrices can be precisely determined by considering the associated Riemann-Hilbert problem. The solution to this problem can be obtained by applying either an algebraic or a geometric method, and in this case, the application of the geometric method seems particularly fitting due to the matrices' solvability; a particular type of matrix function that arises in the problem is shown to be related to a line bundle on a specific type of algebraic variety. The solution to the Riemann-Hilbert problem can be obtained by applying a particular type of deformation to the problem, and the resulting solution can be used to study the asymptotic properties of the solution. The solution to the problem can be obtained by applying a particular type of matrix inversion, and the resulting solution can be used to study the asymptotic properties of the solution. The solution to the problem can be obtained by applying an algebraic method, and the resulting solution can be used to study the asymptotic properties of the solution.

This research investigates the quantum relationships between two particles in a three-state system. By developing a theoretical framework, we derived the matrix-valued generalization of the geometric phase for these particles and identified the condition under which this phase vanishes. Subsequently, we conducted experiments on NMR systems in higher-dimensional spaces to test our theory and measured the geometric phase for various states, including those that transition between different states. The results of our experiments align with our theoretical predictions.

In 1964, Bell formulated his theorem in the form of a mathematical inequality. It was later shown that quantum mechanics violates this inequality under correlations, known as quantum entanglement. This finding led to discussions about the implications for our understanding of space and time. This article presents a new mathematical approach to this issue, distinct from previous methods. It introduces a new inequality that builds upon Bell's, with the addition of a new parameter, alpha. This parameter, when set to 1, returns the original inequality. It is demonstrated that alpha can be 1.1228 or higher in certain experiments involving three parties and four measurement settings. This new parameter is a measure of how certain certain certain correlations can be, particularly when dealing with more than three settings. This new approach offers a way to experimentally verify the departure from the standard framework of quantum mechanics and provides a new tool for studying non-locality in space and time.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a versatile tool for generating diverse high-resolution videos with infinite variety, virtually eliminating repetition and the need for extensive training periods. This breakthrough is achieved through a unique combination of temporal and temporal-temporal cycle-consistency constraints that enhance the model's long-term coherence and short-term creativity. StyleGAN-V is built upon StyleGAN and its development requires minimal modifications to the pre-trained StyleGAN-V model. Our research is the first to integrate temporal-temporal cycle-consistency for video generation, which enables the model to produce more realistic and varied videos with enhanced long-term coherence. This is evident in our extensive evaluation of style and our ablation study demonstrating the benefits of our innovations. StyleGAN-V is now available, and we have successfully applied it to generate a high-resolution video from a single still image in just a few seconds.

Liang Ma and Xuefeng Mao's previous research established that, under the eta correspondence, a specific two-point function transformation in A-type Toda theory is equivalent to a two-point function transformation in the theory of integrable particles, specifically in the context of the S^1-wick orbit of the T^A_m W-algebra. We expand upon this work by investigating function transformations in A-type Toda theory that involve multiple points, and by generalizing the associated two-point function equivalence to transformations in the theory of integrable particles, specifically in the context of the S^1-wick orbit of the T^A_m W-algebra. We further demonstrate that these transformations in the context of integrable particles can be represented by Weyl elements in the hyperoctagon I2, and provide a comprehensive description of the K-orbit corresponding to the S^1-wick orbit of T^A_m W-algebra under the action of the Weyl algebra G_0.

Accurate dose estimation in cancer treatment is crucial for both therapeutic effect and reducing long-term side effects. Current procedures using external radiation therapy techniques involve measuring exposure through indirect methods like thermoluminescent dosimetry (TLD) chips, yet these can be affected by environmental factors and handling. A novel approach combining TLD with deep learning techniques on 3D PET images significantly improves the accuracy of dose estimation in preclinical animal models. This enhanced precision is critical for minimizing normal tissue toxicity in radiation therapy.

In the context of Sobolev-Orlicz spaces within a complete manifold, we explore the solvability of the following nonhomogeneous singular elliptic equation:
  -div$\left(\frac{|{\bf u}|^{p({\bf x})} {\bf u}}{|{\bf u}|^{2}}\right)$div$\left(|{\bf u}|^{g({\bf x})}\right)$=f(|t|) within a domain $\Omega$, t being a point in its interior, the exponents p({\bf x}) and g({\bf x}) varying according to $\alpha$ in the range [0,1], being V-p-regular and V-g-regular respectively, the function f varying with t, the problem being studied under different conditions, the authors proving the existence of a weak solution to this problem.

A computer algorithm was developed to simulate cone beam CT images based on given CT image data, using different X-ray energies and scatter simulation capabilities. The program utilized a cone beam geometric model to calculate primary X-ray paths, then simulated the interaction between X-rays and body tissue, taking into account factors such as photon energy, attenuation, and detector response. The program was validated using patient images taken with different X-ray machines, and was found to accurately simulate images taken with a variety of X-ray energies, including factors such as X-ray scattering.

In this study, we propose S-LIME, a novel method for explaining machine learning models, which builds upon the established LIME technique. S-LIME improves LIME's explanatory power by enhancing its accuracy and stability through a more effective ensemble process utilizing a selection mechanism. The S-LIME approach is then compared to LIME in the context of two benchmark datasets. The results indicate that S-LIME surpasses or equals LIME in terms of explanation quality and stability.

In machine learning, categorization is a fundamental skill, yet current methods often overlook the importance of justifications in the learning process. Our research presents a new categorization framework that not only produces classifications but also provides detailed explanations for its decisions. This framework is based on an innovative Bayesian structure that enables us to efficiently learn and refine categorization skills. The proposed method utilizes a unique approach to combining categorization skills and providing justifications for incorrect classifications. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional categorization techniques in terms of accuracy, generalizability, and ability to correct errors.

TbInO$_3$ is a rare-earth spiral spin-liquid candidate exhibiting unique magnetic properties.  Recent experiments have shown that the compound's magnetic structure is influenced by a unique spin configuration, which is stabilized by a specific type of crystal distortion.  In order to understand the compound's magnetic behavior, we have performed a comprehensive study of its crystal and vibronic excitations using a theoretical approach.  Our calculations indicate that the compound's magnetic crystal excitations are characterized by a specific gap, which is influenced by the type of distortion present.  We also found that the compound's vibronic behavior is highly sensitive to its spin properties and can be used to identify the type of distortion present.  Furthermore, we have identified specific patterns of light absorption that are unique to the compound's spin properties, which are predicted to be observable through experiment.

We apply a novel numerical technique to investigate a family of parabolic mean curvature equations, specifically the power-of-mean curvature evolution equation, which is crucial in the context of mean curvature flow with fixed boundary. This equation plays a significant role in the study of intrinsic geometry and has practical applications in the field of materials science. The method involves a combination of a gradient flow approach and a dynamic boundary condition, where the evolving interface interacts dynamically with the underlying surface. We utilize a convex relaxation framework to transform the non-linear equation into a more manageable convex problem, solving it through a combination of gradient descent and projected gradient descent. The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach are demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments.

A novel approach to learning deep neural networks combines the benefits of frequency domain processing with the end-to-end training capability of deep neural networks. In this study, we investigate a method to train a convolutional neural network in the spectrum domain by utilizing a Fourier transform-based activation function, which enables efficient learning and training of neural network parameters. The proposed model is compared to its time domain counterpart through a series of experiments using speech and audio classification tasks, including noise robustness and classification accuracy evaluation. A comparative analysis of time and frequency domain CNNs reveals that the Fourier domain model excels in noise robustness but is hindered by the vanishing gradient problem due to repeated element activation. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel activation function that leverages the Fourier domain for efficient learning and training of convolutional neural networks.

The task of image clustering is a fundamental challenge in computer vision that has garnered significant attention. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to the development of sophisticated clustering models, which have outperformed traditional methods. However, the existing deep clustering methods primarily focus on a single, linear or non-linear structure within a deep neural network. This paper proposes a new framework, the Deep Clustering Framework, which integrates multiple layers with distinct clustering structures. Our experimental results on standard datasets demonstrate that Deep CluE yields state-of-the-art performance across various evaluation metrics, including the internal and external metrics. Furthermore, the model's scalability is demonstrated by applying it to a pre-trained ResNet-101 and achieving competitive results on the Stl10 dataset.

The potential for risk within an organization is widespread and can manifest in both anticipated and unexpected ways.  The likelihood of unforeseen risks, such as those triggered by current events, is particularly underappended.  This study presents a framework that utilizes news media to identify risks, both anticipated and unexpected, within an organization.  The proposed system is comprised of three primary components: a knowledge network of organizational risks, a risk detection algorithm, and an event tracker.  The knowledge network of organizational risks is populated with risks identified by internal security experts and related risks detected by external organizations, with the latter being gathered through news media aggregation.  The risk detection algorithm utilizes the knowledge network to identify relevant risks, with the results then being disseminated to security experts for evaluation.  The event tracker continuously monitors current events to identify which are related to identified risks, with the information being disseminated to security experts via a risk management platform.

The goal of clustering is to group related data points while separating them from points that belong to different clusters. In this paper, we present a novel clustering method that achieves this goal by analyzing the structure of a high-dimensional data set. Our approach is based on the concept of conditional density that helps identify clusters within high-dimensional data. Our algorithm iteratively refines the density estimates through iterative refinements and constraints, ensuring that the identified clusters are separate and distinct. Our experimental results on real-world data sets demonstrate that our proposed algorithm outperforms other popular clustering methods.

This research paper investigates the contrasimilarity relation, a broadened concept of the similarity relation originally defined on the set of natural numbers. The contrasimilarity relation is established through an extension of finite two-player games with perfect information. The author outlines the rules of these games and describes the contrasimilarity relation as an equilibrium strategy that arises from a simultaneous play of the games. The author then demonstrates that the contrasimilarity relation is the most encompassing relation capable of resolving contradictions that may arise from comparing numbers. Specifically, the author shows that the number of digits in the base-ten representation of two quantities can be compared using the contrasimilarity relation.

We utilize a string 2-group called $\mathrm{G}^{\bullet}(H)$ to represent a gauge theory with a base space that is a manifold $M$, which has a specific structure $H$-bundle $P$ over $M$, and analyze it in terms of an $\mathrm{H}$-gauged string field theory on $M$. The string 2-group $\mathrm{G}^{\bullet}(H)$ is characterized by two group components, a string group component denoted by $\mathrm{G}^{\bullet}$ and a zero component denoted by $H$, and we establish a connection between the string field in the theory and a 2-cocycle of the string 2-group $\mathrm{G}^{\bullet}(H)$. We also derive the action of the theory in terms of this 2-cocycle.

Using double pair plasma with non-extensive particles, we investigate the propagation of ion-acoustic waves, identifying unique features such as rogue pulses. These unique waveforms, characterized by high amplitude and rapid phase, are influenced by variations in plasma parameters and the non-extensive index. By modifying these factors, the appearance of rogue pulses can be controlled. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential for the non-extensive form factor to produce multiple rogue pulses. Our findings have implications for understanding and controlling ion-acoustic waves, with applications in both laboratory experiments and astrophysical environments.

A novel approach to modeling the Alfvén wave parametric decay instability in a plasma is proposed by combining kinetic and fluid models. Starting with the kinetic model, the system's equations are derived and simplified to a set of nonlinear fluid equations. These fluid equations are then solved using a numerical code, where the decay rate of Alfvén waves is tracked in real space and frequency space. The model predictions are compared to a previous kinetic simulation, revealing good agreement. Additionally, the model includes a discussion on the limitations of the fluid approximation and their impact on the outcome of the simulation.

We have investigated the gravitational instability in molecular thread-like nebulae by means of linear analysis, considering the effects of ambipolar diffusion and including the effects of magnetic fields. The analysis revealed that ambipolar diffusion can significantly decrease the gravitational instability threshold, leading to the formation of more prominent density fluctuations. Furthermore, the presence of magnetic fields was found to suppress the instability, with the effects of ambipolar diffusion counteracting these suppressive effects. The results suggest that the formation of star clusters within molecular thread-like nebulae is feasible, with the gravitational instability triggered by the ambipolar diffusion of magnetic flux, leading to the formation of star clusters by gravitational collapse.

The impact of frequent measurements on a quantum system is more pronounced in its early stages than in its later stages, a phenomenon known as the quantum Zeno effect, which is characterized by a system's reduced probability of transitioning into a different state during the measurement process. In contrast, the quantum anti-Zeno effect describes an increase in the transition probability due to the measurements, leading to a greater chance of the system switching to a different state. Both the Zeno and anti-Zeno phenomena have been extensively researched in the context of weak coupling between the system and its environment, but their behavior in the strong coupling regime is not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigate the dynamics of the anti-Zeno effect in the strong coupling regime, specifically with the help of a bosonic environment, and find that the anti-Zeno effect is still present but exhibits distinct features, such as a minimum and maximum in the transition probability. Our findings suggest that the influence of the measurements is more pronounced in the strong coupling regime, and we believe that the unique characteristics of the anti-Zeno effect in this regime may have significant implications for the development of quantum technologies.

This research examines the thermal behavior of a Heisenberg G-type model with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions in a non-uniform external field. We derived the specific heat and magnetization of this model using high-temperature series expansions, specifically up to the 8th and 9th powers of temperature respectively. By comparing these outcomes to comparable results from other studies, we verify their accuracy. Furthermore, we investigate the thermal excitations of this model, specifically the crossover temperatures and low-temperature exponents. We also provide detailed analyses of the specific heat and magnetization plots in various external field conditions.

This study presents a groundbreaking distributed path planning algorithm for quadrotor swarms that ensures safety and viability. The algorithm addresses the challenge of navigating through a group of stationary obstacles in an environment with multiple quadrotors. Each obstacle is associated with a unique entry and exit point known as a "safe passage." The algorithm ensures that the configuration of the quadrotors along the safe passages remains safe and viable at all times. A new viability guarantee method is introduced to prove that the distribution of quadrotors along the safe passages is indeed safe and viable. The method relies on a linear combination of quadrotor positions, which is used to define a viability function. The algorithm ensures that the configuration of quadrotors respects this viability function at all times. Experimental results from simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in ensuring the safety and viability of quadrotor swarms.

Unsupervised learning techniques, such as GAN-based methods, have been successful in adapting simulation-based policies to real-world environments. Although prior studies have focused on adapting specific policies, they have not addressed the more complex issue of unsupervised learning between simulation and diverse real-world environments. In this study, we introduce CARLANE, a benchmark for unsupervised learning across various real-world domains, and provide a comprehensive analysis of the challenges associated with it. By offering a large, diverse dataset of 12 real-world domains and a baseline comparison, we aim to facilitate further research on adapting simulation-based policies to real-world settings.

Our research focuses on how nanoparticles affect contact angle solidification on hydrogel surfaces. The presence of these particles leads to a noticeable, quantifiable rise in contact angle compared to hydrogel alone. By combining hydrogel with silica particles of varying sizes and concentrations, we explore the particle's impact on wettability. Theoretical predictions were made using a modified Young's equation, taking into account the wettability of the particle and hydrogel interstitial space. Through this model, we discovered that larger particles and higher particle loads can amplify the increase in contact angle. Furthermore, we observed that the particle size's influence on contact angle follows a logarithmic relationship.

The abrupt shift to online learning brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted higher education, causing a decline in participation among students during the summer of 2020. Building on existing research, which analyzed the relationship between student engagement and academic performance among students transitioning to online learning during the spring of 2020, this study extended this investigation to encompass the full year of 2020-2021 and an additional year of data collection. Our analysis of a large dataset of students from a prominent US public university revealed that, similar to previous findings, student engagement was a strong indicator of academic performance during the pandemic year. Our results also showed that students who were more engaged had better outcomes compared to their peers, even after considering demographic and prior academic factors. This study further solidified the link between student engagement and academic performance during the pandemic while providing insights into how the pandemic affected students and its lasting impact on their academic year.

The wind's influence on spacecraft orientation is a major concern for satellite operations in orbit, and the Swift observatory's 78-foot wind anemometer provides regular readings. However, the Swift spacecraft is equipped with a range of sensitive instruments, which are vulnerable to disruption caused by wind vibrations. To address this issue, researchers have developed a statistical model that takes into account the wind's impact on the solar monitor and one of the X-ray telescopes. By applying this model to historical wind data, they were able to accurately predict the effects of different wind speeds on the solar monitor and one of the X-ray telescopes. By analyzing the wind's patterns and patterns of variation, researchers found that their statistical approach was effective in predicting wind influences on the solar monitor and one of the X-ray telescopes.

We conducted a thorough investigation of the open cluster UBC 274, utilizing data from Gaia EDR3, which revealed the cluster's disrupted state. By applying the maximum likelihood method, we determined the kinematic properties of the cluster's remnants, discovering that its tidal radius exceeds 15 pc and the cluster's mass is approximately $1.45 \times 10^{3} M_{\odot}$. Our analysis also revealed that the cluster's remnants show a significant velocity dispersion within the 10-20 pc radius, which is approximately 4.5 km/s. Furthermore, we observed a metallicity decrease from approximately solar values at the center to sub-solar values towards the periphery. Additionally, we identified a significant star-to-star elemental variation in elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, which is likely a result of the cluster's disruption. Our analysis suggests that the cluster's disruption occurred approximately 300 million years ago, which is significantly earlier than the cluster's age, which is approximately 650 million years and is consistent with the cluster's kinematic properties.

The primary metric for assessing machine translation (MT) performance is BLEU score. However, this evaluation is merely a reflection of MT's capabilities and does not directly measure the performance of MT models in supporting NLP tasks. In this study, we investigate whether an MT model can be utilized to enhance the quality of a pre-existing multilingual corpus. We examine this possibility by training a MT model on a set of high-quality parallel corpora and employing it to generate synthetic parallel samples, which we integrate into a low-quality multilingual corpus. The resulting corpus is evaluated using a range of NLP tasks, including language modeling, machine translation, and word similarity, and our findings indicate that this enhanced corpus surpasses the original one.

We explore the concept of engineered dissipation, where a system is driven into a specific quantum state by deliberately inducing dissipation, using a quantum spin chain as a model. By applying a dissipation field to a specific site, we investigate how the system's behavior changes in different ground states and edge conditions. Our results show that the system's behavior is influenced by the system's size and the type of edge conditions it has, and that the system's behavior is shifted from one ground state to another by controlling the dissipation field. Our results also show that the system's behavior is influenced by the system's length and the type of edge conditions it has, and that the system's behavior is shifted from one ground state to another by controlling the dissipation field. Our findings indicate that the system's behavior is influenced by the system's length and the type of edge conditions it has, and that the system's behavior is shifted from a logarithmic increase to a constant value. Our results have implications for the study of quantum state transfer and the control of quantum systems.

A unique characteristic of two-dimensional materials is the presence of flat energy bands, with a minimal bandgap. The interplay between flat bands and spin-orbit effects is crucial in determining the properties of both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials. In this research, we investigate the spin-orbit interaction in a specific type of layered materials known as transition metal dichalcogenides. We have developed a computational framework to model the electronic and magnetic properties of these materials, with a focus on their heterostructures. Our results show that the flat bands in these materials are susceptible to significant spin-orbit effects, with a range of spin-dependent parameters that can be adjusted. We have also identified a specific configuration where the flat bands merge into a single band with strong spin-orbit effects, with potential applications in spintronic devices.

A novel quantum filtering approach has been formulated to analyze and process quantum systems with reduced complexity, utilizing a framework based on probability theory rather than differential equations. This method, known as quantum reservoir processing, is particularly effective in managing and processing quantum information in systems with restricted dimensions. This approach provides a unified understanding of both continuous and discrete quantum filtering, and it enables the creation of new algorithms tailored to specific filtering tasks in systems with reduced dimensions.

The development of a single-photon source, utilizing an atom trapped within a nanocavity, has garnered significant attention. This concept, though proven in theory with high efficiency, has been hindered by the limitations of material, such as poor quality silicon and insulator combined with high-refractive-index GaAs. A novel approach to create a reliable single-photon source employs a GaN-on-sapphire substrate, as it allows for the use of a previously demonstrated high-quality GaN quantum well. This process involves the creation of a nanocavity by etching GaN down to a thickness of 20 nm. However, the main challenge lies in preventing GaN from creeping into the etched region, as it would significantly compromise the confinement of the quantum well. A proposed solution involves the implementation of a sapphire seed layer, as it would act as a barrier to prevent GaN from creeping into the etched region, allowing for the successful creation of a single-photon source.

This research introduces a finite element method study for solving the Laplace equation, examining both Lagrange and mixed elements in conjunction with various numerical methods. The performance of this model was investigated across different problem settings, including the 2D and 3D scenarios, where the unique characteristics of mixed elements were demonstrated in 2D. Additionally, an example of mixed elements in a 3D porous medium was presented, highlighting the ability to link pressure and flux as simulated discretely. The study's results, generated using the MFEM software library, are presented and discussed.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of two distinct dark energy models with sign-alterable interactions, which involve a phantom line and phantom anti-brane setup in a specific space. This setting includes a scalar field with a dynamic model, a time-dependent Lagrangian, and a coupling factor that changes over time. By applying the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric, we find the equations of motion for the coupled system and analyze key parameters, including the Hubble parameter, deceleration parameter, statefinder diagnostics, and jerk and jasper numbers, which show that the models can explain the universe's evolution from an initially decelerated state to a currently accelerated one.

The observed radio bursts from TDE events may be linked to the phenomenon of perpendicular shock waves in the interstellar medium. The compression of ambient electrons in the shock wave can release energy in the form of synchrotron radiation, which can be detected as a radio burst. The rate at which these bursts occur, and their distribution in the light curve, can be predicted based on the frequency of shock encounters by high velocity TDE outflows. The energy output of these shock waves can be significant, potentially exceeding the energy released by the deceleration process. Theoretical models of shock wave effects on the TDE jet suggest that the energy output could be substantial, which could have implications for understanding the observed radio bursts from TDE events. Theoretical light curves were generated based on the frequency of shock encounters, which can be compared to the observed light curves of several TDE events.

The research introduces a mathematical model for acoustic cavitation, focusing on the interaction between acoustic waves and a limited number of micro-bubbles within a confined medium. The model is formulated in the time domain using the Keller-Hayden-Michalakis framework, accounting for the transient behavior of bubble oscillations and non-linear bubble-wall interactions. The developed model is utilized to analyze the acoustic response of a single micro-bubble attached to a stiff surface subjected to a low-intensity, pulsed acoustic wave, with special emphasis on the effects of bubble resonance and driving force direction.

In our research, we introduce a novel, multi-modal method, known as MUSER, aimed at identifying tension in human-computer interactions. MUSER leverages a dataset that combines acknowledged affective expressions with physical characteristics of the computer as input, and learns tension recognition as a unified, multi-modal task. MUSER outperforms a single-modal approach by utilizing an emotion acknowledgment task to enhance its training, resulting in a 10% improvement in multi-modal performance and a 5% improvement in single-modal performance. Our investigation into tension recognition reveals notable disparities in the patterns of tension and normal interactions, particularly in interaction duration, speed, and mouse movements.

We introduce PanGEA, an advanced data annotation tool, to facilitate more
realistic and efficient reinforcement learning in graph-based environments.
By utilizing an external simulator, PanGEA efficiently generates large-scale
graph simulations based on predefined specifications, thereby allowing for
unbiased training data collection. Unlike traditional methods requiring manual
reward assignments, PanGEA automates the annotation process, thus providing
scalable training data for agents learning to navigate complex graph-based
scenarios. Our toolkit is adaptable to a wide range of graph applications,
enabling researchers to create customized environments, collect data, and
evaluate performance.

We have developed a new model to study the evolution of elliptical galaxies by considering the variation in the star formation rate over time, the impact of star formation on the interstellar medium, and the effect of this medium on the formation of new stars. This model also takes into account the influence of supernovae and calculates the mass of metals produced, allowing us to compare our results with observations of elliptical galaxies including their stellar populations and the mass of metals present. The model accounts for how the type of stars formed can vary depending on the environment, with more massive stars produced in denser areas and more long-lived stars produced in less dense areas. This variation affects the mass of metals produced, with more of these elements being produced in denser areas. The model also shows that the mass of stars produced, the mass of metals produced, and the mass of energy produced by these stars all increase over time, with the mass of stars produced, the mass of metals produced, and the mass of energy produced at a certain point in time being approximately 20%, 30%, and 60% of the total mass of the galaxy, respectively. The model also shows that the mass of supernovae occurring at a certain point in time is 10% of the total mass of the galaxy, that the mass of metals produced is 30% of the total mass of the galaxy, and that the mass of stars produced is 50% of the total mass of the galaxy.
